passages.happening:
“And the boy Samuel ministered to the LORD before Eli. Now in those days the word of the LORD was rare and visions were scarce” (verse 1).

Eli's eyes have grown so dim that he cannot see. He is lying in his room. ‘Before the lamp of God had gone out, Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was located’ (verse 3).

The LORD calls Samuel, and the boy answers, “Here I am.” He runs to Eli: “Here I am, for you have called me.” “I did not call,” Eli replied. “Go back and lie down” (verse 5). It happens a second time, and a third. ‘Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, because the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him’ (verse 7).

At the third call Eli understands that it is the LORD calling the boy. He tells Samuel to lie down and, if he is called again, to answer the LORD as his servant who is listening (verse 9). Then the LORD comes and stands there and calls as before, “Samuel! Samuel!” And Samuel answers, “Speak, for Your servant is listening” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
These are still the last years of Eli at Shiloh, in the eleventh century BC. The book of Judges had few prophets. Deborah is called a prophetess, and an unnamed prophet appears once, but most of the book belongs to fighters. So the first verse describes a long silence. Worship went on at Shiloh, but God rarely spoke, and the text suggests that the corrupt priesthood was part of the reason.

The lamp of God was the lampstand in the sanctuary, which the priests kept burning from evening until morning. Saying it had not yet gone out places the call in the dark hours before dawn. The scene is dark in more ways than one: Eli cannot see, the word of the LORD is rare, and the lamp is burning low.

Samuel sleeps in the temple, where the ark is kept. Some readers think he slept in a room in the sanctuary buildings rather than beside the ark itself, since only the high priest entered the most holy place. The Hebrew allows either picture.

In the ancient world many believed that the gods spoke through dreams, and some people slept in temples hoping for a message. Samuel is not seeking anything. The LORD comes and stands and calls him by name, in a voice the boy takes for a man's.

The chapter is built on threes. Three times the LORD calls, three times Samuel runs to Eli with the same words, and three times Eli sends him back. The repeating builds suspense and a little humor, and it shows the boy's readiness and his inexperience. Then the old priest whose eyes have failed is the one who sees what is happening, and he teaches the boy how to answer.
passages.later:
Samuel's ‘Here I am’ is the answer Abraham gave when God called him (Genesis 22:1), and Moses at the burning bush, where God also called his name twice, “Moses, Moses!” (Exodus 3:4). Isaiah gave the same kind of answer: “Here am I. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8).

Amos later warns of a time like the one in verse 1, ‘a famine of hearing the words of the LORD’ (Amos 8:11).
passages.asks: Samuel heard the voice three times and still thought it was Eli. Ask who has helped you recognize God's voice when you could not tell it from any other. And ask whether you are ready to say ‘Speak, for Your servant is listening’ before you know what will be said.

passages.t: A hard word, and an old man's answer
passages.happening:
The LORD tells Samuel, “I am about to do something in Israel at which the ears of all who hear it will tingle” (verse 11). He will carry out everything he said against Eli's family. “I told him that I would judge his house forever for the iniquity of which he knows, because his sons blasphemed God and he did not restrain them” (verse 13). And God has sworn that the guilt of Eli's house will never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering (verse 14).

Samuel lies down until morning and then opens the doors of the house of the LORD. ‘He was afraid to tell Eli the vision’ (verse 15).

But Eli calls him: “Samuel, my son.” Samuel answers, “Here I am” (verse 16). Eli presses him to hide nothing, and puts the boy under a solemn oath to tell all (verse 17).

‘So Samuel told him everything and did not hide a thing from him’ (verse 18). “He is the LORD,” replied Eli. “Let Him do what is good in His eyes” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The first word God gives Samuel is not a comfort. It is a judgment on the household that raised him, and it repeats what the man of God had already told Eli in chapter 2. The warning had gone unheeded.

Eli's oath in verse 17, ‘May God punish you, and ever so severely’, was a standard way of binding someone. It called down a curse on the speaker if he failed to do what was asked. Eli uses it to make the boy tell him the whole message.

Samuel is afraid, and no wonder. The message is about the man who taught him to listen. He tells it anyway, and he tells all of it.

Eli's answer has been read in two ways. Some hear humble faith, an old man bowing to God's justice. Others hear a tired resignation from a man who had heard the same warning before and still did not act. The text does not say which.
passages.later:
The prophets used the same picture for coming disaster. Of the judgment on Jerusalem in Manasseh's day, God says ‘the news will reverberate in the ears of all who hear it’ (2 Kings 21:12), and through Jeremiah, ‘the ears of all who hear of it will ring’ (Jeremiah 19:3).

The word against Eli's house was carried out in stages, and its last stage came under Solomon, when Abiathar was removed from the priesthood (1 Kings 2:27).
passages.hard:
Why does God say that the guilt of Eli's house will never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering? Is this an unforgivable sin?

The statement sounds like one, and readers find it troubling. In its setting, the sacrifices are exactly what Eli's sons have abused and despised. Verse 14 says that the very offerings they treated with contempt will not cover them. The judgment concerns the priestly family's office and its future, and it is announced as fixed because the warning of chapter 2 went unheeded.

Readers differ on whether it shuts out a person's repentance. Some read it as a judgment on the house as an institution, which does not decide the eternal state of each member of the family. Others compare it with the law's words on defiant sin: “But the person who sins defiantly, whether a native or foreigner, blasphemes the LORD” (Numbers 15:30), sin for which the sacrifices gave no remedy. Either way, the chapter's concern is the public judgment on a corrupt priesthood, and it presents that judgment as just.

No one should read this verse as a verdict on themselves.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Samuel was afraid to tell Eli the truth, and told it anyway. Ask whether there is a hard word you owe someone, said with care and without softening it into nothing. And ask how you receive a hard word yourself: as Eli did, or by turning toward God.

passages.happening:
“And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him, and He let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground” (verse 19).

“So all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was confirmed as a prophet of the LORD” (verse 20).

“And the LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, because there He revealed Himself to Samuel by His word” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The chapter began with the word of the LORD rare. It ends with the word of the LORD established. That frame is the chapter's message: God has not abandoned Israel, and he has begun to speak again.

‘He let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground’ means that nothing Samuel said in God's name failed. Every word came true. The law of Moses had given that as a test: a message given in the LORD's name that does not come true ‘is a message the LORD has not spoken’ (Deuteronomy 18:22).

From Dan to Beersheba named the northern and southern edges of Israel's land, about 150 miles apart. It became a common way of saying the whole country. Samuel is no longer only a boy at one shrine in Ephraim. All Israel knows him.
passages.later:
A psalm remembers Samuel as a man of prayer: ‘Samuel was among those who called on His name. They called to the LORD and He answered’ (Psalm 99:6).

Peter, preaching in Jerusalem, names him at the head of the prophets: “Indeed, all the prophets from Samuel on, as many as have spoken, have proclaimed these days” (Acts 3:24).
passages.asks: The chapter begins with God's word rare and ends with it spoken again. Ask where the word of God has grown rare in your own life, and what it would take to listen again. And ask whether the words you say in God's name are words you could stand behind.
